utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber owes a decision to the Prosecution. The Prosecution has requested to reconsider the time available for the Prosecution for cross-examination of Witness DP35. The Chamber will grant to a very limited extent the request. That means that the Prosecutor -- the Prosecution has another 20 minutes net time for cross-examination. "Net time" means that interruptions, whatever, will not be part of those 20 minutes. So 20 minutes effective time for further cross-examination. Among others, the Chamber has taken into consideration the efficiency of the time -- the efficiency with which the time available was used. The Chamber has in mind, for example, that coming to the rhythm of firing of a 40-millimetre weapon, it might have not taken half an hour to get there through 20, 30, and then finally 40-millimetre. The Chamber also has taken into consideration that the presentation of the Prosecutor's case primarily should take place during the first part of the trial. And of course, the Prosecution is entitled, just as the Defence was, to take advantage of Rule 90(H) in order to present relevant parts of its own case if one can expect that a witness has knowledge of it, but that would not justify a firm expectation of what can be expected from the other party in respect of calling witnesses. If they are called, Rule 90(H) applies. If they're finally not called, the Prosecution will have to rely on time available for the case presentation at the beginning of the trial. The Chamber has granted extra time in respect of Witness DP35 already because the Chamber sees that this witness is not without importance for the Prosecution. It grants another 20 minutes, and then we'll move on. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Witness DP35 into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. DP35.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The cross-examination by counsel will now continue. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Ierace: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you have told us that vehicles in military and vehicles for which you had reason to believe they were carrying weapons or explosives were legitimate targets. Were there any other types of vehicles that were legitimate targets? And I'm talking about cars.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stressed that these vehicles were field vehicles or lorries. This was not about larger-type vehicles, at least in the area that I was able to follow it in in those directions. There were no light vehicles. There were no passenger cars, passenger vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that you were responsible for the anti-aircraft weaponry and training of the crews of those weapons. What would be your attitude towards those crews targeting any car in the city on the other side of the confrontation lines? Do you think that appropriate or inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think it inappropriate, and I have already stressed that they were not in a possibility to fire on the town in the urban, in the densely populated part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us in some detail about the types of rounds that could be fired by anti-aircraft weaponry and in particular how 90 per cent of those rounds were of the explosive type, so that once fired they would inevitably explode. Do you agree that if such fire was directed indiscriminately into the city, it would terrorise the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object. I have to object in the way that the question was phrased. It seems to confirm that the troops would have been firing at the town in an indiscriminate fashion. And the position of this witness was completely the opposite. So it's in the contradiction to the previous testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I invite you to read the question, and especially the use of the word "if." To me it quite clearly contemplates a hypothetical situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- in cross-examination it is permissible to raise a situation, even if this does not reflect entirely the testimony of the witness until that moment. Please proceed. So would you please answer that question that if such rounds that would necessarily explode before -- if that would be fired to the city, that this would terrorise the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. I have stressed that we did not fire from three barrels but from two. We didn't use long bursts of fire but short bursts of fire or single-mode fire. So the priority when opening fire was efficiency, effectiveness, and saving of ammunition. So it would be completely pointless for me to allow units or sections to open fire in an indiscriminate fashion, unselectively. So I am answering your question that I did not allow it and I was not in a position to open -- or to follow such inselective fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You misunderstand my question. If there had been indiscriminate use of those weapons, if they had been fired across the city indiscriminately, do you accept that in that circumstance inevitably such firing would terrorise the civilian population of Sarajevo; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have caused the terrorising of the population, but we did not do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us earlier in your evidence that you received protests passed on through the liaison officer of the SRK. Was that Major Indjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those protests relate to civilians being targeted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stressed those cases for which I knew and described in my statements, and in any case there were also cases where there was the allegation that civilians were targeted. But these cases were not within the -- my authority in the work of the command, so I could have been informed about this but I did not discuss them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you are able to answer my questions with a simple yes or no, then please do so. We don't have a lot of time. Did Major Indjic attend the meetings you have described at the operations centre on a daily basis that you attended with General Galic and other senior subordinates; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about a particular protest which involved a UN officer, and I think you said his name was Kolp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Kolp expressed gratitude for the investigation carried out by the SRK in relation to that particular incident. Was that relationship with Kolp typical of the relationship that the SRK enjoyed with UNPROFOR in relation to protests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one case. I believe that there were more than one, but I cannot guarantee if I wasn't present whether there was satisfaction expressed or gratitude by the UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you attended these daily senior meetings which reviewed operations. As far as you're aware, was there a good relationship between UNPROFOR and the SRK command in relation to protests or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was good cooperation and a good relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by Mr. Piletta-Zanin whether protests included such precise information as the exact locations of alleged victims, and you said that the protests did not. Did that cause any difficulty for the SRK in carrying out its investigations; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, in view of the good relationship did the relevant SRK personnel simply not ask UNPROFOR for the relevant further information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further information was requested, but in most of the cases it had to -- things had to happen very quickly to reach a conclusion very quickly about what had really happened, and that's why there were problems. If there was a very wide area that was given, it was very difficult to decide on a precise location and about what victims, exactly where, and as to what was said to the representative of the defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, who was it in the SRK who primarily dealt with UNPROFOR in relation to protests? Was it Indjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, with his associates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any reason as to why he and his associates could have not requested that further information when first informed of the protest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason not to request further information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did General Galic ever in the relevant period tell you that he had personally received a protest involving civilian victims from UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that he had directly received it, but again, protests went through the office of the liaison officer, and they were forwarded to General Galic, that is, to the operation centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please listen to the question. I'm not asking you what typically happened. I'm asking you whether General Galic ever told you in the relevant period that he had personally received a protest involving civilian victims from UNPROFOR. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that reports were generated as a result of these investigations. You said the reports were forwarded to the main staff of the VRS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those reports -- yes. Yes, they were. They were forwarded, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you expect those reports to be with the archive of the SRK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parts of the reports that were to be found in daily combat reports -- so these were summaries of parts of reports that were done by the liaison officer -- were in any case in daily combat reports, as this was the case yesterday, the one where we discussed item number 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean by that that there were not separate reports in relation to these investigations but, rather, references to them in the combat reports? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A separate report went along the route through the liaison officer with UNPROFOR, and this is the line that the detailed report followed. But a summarised, shortened version of a report was put as an item within the daily combat report entitled "Relationship with UNPROFOR."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you do mean that there were not separate reports that went to the main staff but, rather, references to the reports incorporated in the daily combat report. Is that correct? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I wanted to say is what I said, that following the line of the office of the liaison officer, those reports went to the main staff because it was in the main staff that the liaison officer was. And along that line he was superior to Indjic. Indjic did that report for that officer in the main staff and also --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Do you know where those reports are today; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us that reports went to UNPROFOR. Were they written reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that is incorrect, that written reports in relation to such protests were not given to UNPROFOR. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am convinced that they did go. You probably have different information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of anyone, anyone at all being charged as a result of an investigation carried out within the SRK in the relevant period for unlawful behaviour resulting in the injury or death of civilians on the other side of the confrontation line; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to know whether any of these protests that were received alleged anti-aircraft fire into the city. And I appreciate you have already told us that your weapons could not reach the city on the other side. Nevertheless, were there such protests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that there were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me an example, please. Explain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that throughout the relevant period protests were made by UNPROFOR which involved the use of anti-aircraft fire into the city. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has already answered the question very clearly, asking the Prosecution to give an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's exactly that answer that permits the Prosecution to ask it again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the state hospital was a regular recipient of anti-aircraft fire from the area of Vrace in the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, here -- no, no the chronology -- I withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree. This is the first time I hear that the state hospital was targeted from Vrace. Yes, it was within the range, but we never even saw the hospital, if, that is, you're talking about Kosevo hospital, we never even saw the Kosevo hospital from Vrace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your positions on the map, I suggest to you, from the anti-aircraft --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, yes, Kosevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a confusion as to what hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is directed to the state hospital, not the Kosevo hospital. Are you aware of the existence in the relevant period of the state hospital? Previously known as the military hospital, sometimes known as the French hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I understand. Yes, it is the military hospital. The military hospital could be within the range, but it could not be seen from any Vrace position or any other position on this side, as I showed you on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that that answer and indeed the positions you marked on the map are the anti-aircraft units mean little in view of the inherent mobility of those units. In other words, they could be very easily moved around. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They could move about, but they were obstacles which prevented it from firing at -- rather, hitting the state hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now, on Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve 1992, where were you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we need chronological precision. We need this to be stated more precisely chronologically. Shall I repeat that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. But Christmas Eve 1992, I take it that's the 24th or 25th at night. Is that what you -- Oh, yes, yes. I do understand. I apologise. Christmas is not a unambiguous expression in this respect, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to Serbian Orthodox New Year's Eve 1992, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the 24th of December, 1992, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992? On Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On Christmas Eve, according to the Serbian Orthodox calendar in 1992, where were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992? I told you. I was in Mostar. And for Christmas, the Catholic Christmas, on the 24th of December, I was in Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you that on Christmas Eve, 24th of December, on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stroke of midnight there was a barrage lasting some 20 minutes of artillery, mortar, tank, and machine-gun fire into the city, including the firing of a 40-millimetre Bofor anti-aircraft gun. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that because I did not discuss this case, whether a 40-millimetre fired. Then it was done beyond my control without my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- From Trebevic, you would have heard it, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your absence at Mostar, on the other two evenings, I suggest to you exactly the same behaviour occurred and it could not have occurred without you knowing about it. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think there is some confusion. I believe there is some confusion again. If we're talking about 1992 January and the witness's stay in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's perhaps put it in a different way to the witness. Mr. DP35, are you aware of an event approximately 20 minutes of artillery, mortar, tank, and machine-gun fire on either Orthodox or Catholic Christmas or New Year's Eve --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, including anti-aircraft fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Including anti-aircraft fire. So does such a barrage - I'm asking for 20 minutes at one of these days - ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can ring a bell, but now I cannot associate that event with any special importance. I do not see why it was so important. I was on Trebevic at the time under the regiment command post, and I was given no warning that there was any fire opened or that the firing was done by a unit under my command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're talking about -- we are talking about a barrage that lasted some 20 minutes and a large number of weaponry firing approximately at the same time for 20 minutes. Do you have any recollection that such a thing happened? Whether it was important in your view or not is a different matter, but did such a thing happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have two small objections. We have -- we are keeping our eye on the clock, and it is now already more than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I said net time. Please proceed. Yes. The second issue you wanted --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that is it. I think that the time has expired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I suggest to you that throughout the relevant period anti-aircraft fire deliberately or recklessly fired at civilians in Sarajevo on the other side of the confrontation line. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that you moved around the area as well as spending time in the operations centre. Did you not see erected throughout the city barricades at intersections consisting of containers, blankets, sheets and the like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never saw that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the opposite side, no. I saw them on our side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the existence of such barricades at any stage through the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about their existence, but I could not see them on the Muslim side. On our side they existed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that you knew about their existence on the other side of the confrontation line during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could see them only along the Miljacka, that is, right next to the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could I ask you to conclude in one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That will cover it, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need for the Defence to re-examine the witness? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning. I'd like to go back to what you just said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And will the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a lot of talk about protests which were made, and there were such questions yesterday. And today I'd like to suggest to you the following -- we shall have read out names which are presumably all civilian, and then my question will be: Have you ever seen these names in any protest whatever? I will now read them now, and if any of those names rings a bell, you will please tell us so. [redacted], Anisa Pita --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If those names relate to the indictment, I'd ask my learned colleague to be sure that he doesn't offend any protective orders in relation to the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But before continuing, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. DP35, have you any knowledge or is -- do you have any recollection in respect of names of civilian victims or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the Muslim side, you mean? No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have -- no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that answer all the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about protests, witness, the question that we'll ask in this relation - I never said it precisely - whether those were general protests concerning alleged illegitimate shelling or quite the contrary, if these protests were general or specific concerning sniping, the protests that -- the rare protests which are mentioned in your answer, did they concern the protests concerning shelling or something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I? I've already mentioned the specific case of the fire opened at the tower. There it was precisely said what had been hit. And it was also pointed out, and I said, that it was the rocket launcher. And on my position there were no rocket launcher, so I said that that was not the case. I also mentioned the shelling of Dobrinja. The checking was done, and it was completed as I have pointed out. There was general reference to Markale, but there was no specific location. The number of casualties ranged between a few to several dozens. I know. I remember that. Through the liaison officer, cooperation was offered with the opposite side to investigate the case, but in that case we did not receive an answer in the affirmative, and personally I was not concerned with this because my men could not participate in this, that is, my men and the subordinate units, but those associates of mine who were to take part in this and who stood ready to do that did not because their cooperation was not accepted in order to establish the facts. I presume somebody didn't really want to have the truth properly established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. I'd like us now to try to synthesise, therefore, the examples you gave us, and possibly since I said that you are a witness concerned mostly shellings. Is that how I should understand your testimony? They mostly had to do with shellings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. By and large those were shellings, or perhaps the use of rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Thank you. Witness, when investigations were conducted, you told us that they had to be conducted under wartime conditions. Could you give us some details concerning the manner in which those investigations were conducted. How did this happen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That does not arise out of cross-examination. I didn't get to that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This does arise from cross-examination because the witness said that when -- that it was very difficult to do this because the time was limited. It was a wartime situation, that one needed to try to establish the facts straight away. So it does arise from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, no question was asked of this witness in cross-examination about the modus of the investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But a question was asked whether the lack of data was any --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Impediment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Impediment to the investigation. To that extent the Defence is allowed to ask to a limited extent questions on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As you please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you give us some details. How did you go about this? Was it always possible to do it? And so on and so forth, if you know it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in case of the Butmir sports air field, it was not in dispute, because there were those positions from which it could be fired at from our side, so that UNPROFOR officers and senior officers could go there safely in our presence, in my presence, and escorted by the unit that was there. It was more difficult to go to the opposite side. I mean, for our representatives, even with guarantees, because UNPROFOR was unable to ensure the safe conduct for our representatives to that side in order to check particular sites. And I suppose that was why our men were not incorporated in the investigation either in Dobrinja or in Markale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in this particular last case, was it very difficult to investigate the latest element, that is, the fact that it was impossible to go check the site? Did it make it very difficult to establish facts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons why things remained salient. Although, there are certain things which confirm what I said earlier; namely, that the accusations were false.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, now I'd like us to focus on another matter and that is a document which we looked at yesterday, the order which came from General Galic and whose item 3 was general instruction to observe to comply with the Geneva Conventions. Do you remember this document? It was 1491 -- no, excuse me, 1492. And this is a document which you had the opportunity to read yesterday. Do you recall that document, and could that document be given you once again. 1492.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is now under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document should not be put on -- placed on the ELMO, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, but we can -- we can indeed -- we can deal with it without putting it on the ELMO because I think we all recall this document. I need the witness to have it before his eyes. It does not have to be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to ascertain that we're talking about the same document, witness, I'm referring to item 3. However, before that, before that I'd like you to read aloud the items 1 and 2. Can you do that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 1: "Enable unfettered passage and protection of parcels, equipment, and personnel, extending help to the civilian population of the opposite side." 2: "Prohibit the misuse for military purposes of foodstuffs, crop, water mains, and reserve drinking water, and dams in hydro powerplants." Item 3 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now will you please be so kind as to read the beginning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The order for an unfettered passage of humanitarian relief to all units of SRK on the basis of the directive, doesn't really matter, 1993, order of the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska under the indicated number in order to maintain to support the signed cease-fire from our side and consistent implementation of the directive as --" and then follows the text that I have just read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Yesterday you said in relation to item 3 that you'd rather not comment on this item. Can you tell us why did you give that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. In fact, the witness said that during examination-in-chief. And in essence, my friend has just re-asked the question that I asked the witness yesterday. So this is not a proper question for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor has, following the answers of the witness, asked a number of questions of the witness in order to find out whether the witness knew or did not know what was in these documents and to show that this witness, like the other officers who were under him, were aware of this, and that is why we believe the Defence has the right to ask these questions of the witness and that is why we ask him to read them. And what I am reading was the work which was done by the Prosecution during the cross-examination, and I'm asking the witness because he declined to give the answer to that, and therefore, I'm trying to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I could. My friend, with respect, misses the point. It was during his questioning of this witness that the witness said he could not comment on point 3. If my friend wanted to find out why he could not comment, he could have done that in chief. The question he has just asked the witness is one that I asked in cross-examination. It is inappropriate in re-examination, secondly, to simply re-ask the same questions asked in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of my problems is - and that might be the problem for the parties as well - that we have not in this courtroom the transcript available of what happened yesterday. So if one of the parties could provide me with the relevant -- it has been loaded this morning. So I am, as always, behind. It was asked to the witness in chief yesterday, Mr. -- The day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The day before yesterday. And I have copy of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could please provide that -- the relevant source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed that we have the day before yesterday as well. I should first open that. Could you please point at the -- at the page number, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I printed it off yesterday, it was page 59 of the draft LiveNote. This is for the 14th of January. The time was approximately 11.59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll do a search in the transcript. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the word "comment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I had in mind. The witness responded to a question of you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that he could not comment on it. So the reasons why he could not comment on it could have been asked by you at that very moment. The witness gave extensive information on the circumstances of the documents, so the issue on whether or not the witness could comment on it and the further elaboration of that do not arise from cross-examination but from the examination-in-chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, Mr. President. Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after you said that you would rather not comment, the Prosecution asked you some questions concerning this item 3. And I am referring now to the question asked by the Prosecution which had to do with this item 3. You stated in response to these questions that in your opinion, you would have judged it useless to redact, to redraft this item 3. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please explain to the Chamber why did you say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have an electronic copy of the -- or any copy of the transcript from yesterday because of the change of courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll search for the -- they have been loaded this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I simply don't recollect any comment by the witness that he thought it pointless to redraft the item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not my recollection either. I think the word -- there might have been things useless but not redrafting. At least that's not my recollection. But if you could indicate where to find that, Mr. -- I think the witness testified yesterday that he would have drafted the order in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm asking the witness, and the witness said yes. I've just asked the question, and the witness has said yes. So I think that his best place to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's a matter of -- the objection of Mr. Ierace was that you misrepresented the evidence, and the usual way of solving such a problem is to look at the transcript. And if you think that the transcript is not correct in this respect - and I was just trying to search for it - then of course we always called --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I ask the Prosecution according to the usual rule to quote the passage where the witness did not say this, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can't quote a passage if someone does not say it. If there's an objection, you should refer to the place where --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Mr. President. This is rather hard. What I wanted to ask him is to quote the passage, but I will do it differently. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what did you say, please, yesterday in relation to the need or lack of need to do in relation to item 3? Can you remind us of that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I would not have put in, written, item 3 because the subordinate units, that is, the commanders from the subordinate units, do not have time to study in detail -- to remind themselves of the decisions or certain parts of the Geneva Conventions, particularly if this is in relation to implementing the task or carrying out the tasks which are completely clear, both in item 1 and item 2, that are unambiguous. So what I said is that there was no possibility for us not even to carry the most basic rules in documents let alone any expanded rules. So I'd like to add to my answer in the following way, because I've thought about it, and I know what I said: That on several occasions when there was time, there were certain parts that were forwarded that are important, relate to war conflicts, important for the subordinate units, and I know this did figure. So what I am saying: Regardless of how much I knew things by heart - and of course, you cannot know things by heart without having these documents, Geneva Conventions in your hands, or even certain parts - what I'm saying is that the introductory part from the order which refers to the Presidency and the main staff, that was enough for me, that this was written by a certain category of people who are literate and they know what they're referring to. They're referring to the Geneva Conventions. Therefore -- that's what I said. It's for subordinate units. What would have been enough were items 1 and 2, not that item 3 was completely superfluous. Items 1 and 2 are sufficient. Item 3 is not completely superfluous. But what I said is not that we didn't understand it. What I'm saying is that it wasn't necessary to study it as such, to go into details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Now, what have you to say about the knowledge that the other officers had or did not have in relation to the conventions mentioned in item 3 -- and that in the course of cross-examination. Now, in relation to that, the question is the followings -- I'm not talking about the details, about the word-for-word recollection of the convention. But the essence, the essence of the convention that was mentioned in item 3, is it known to you? Are you familiar with it? And did other officers in the corps know about this? Did they know it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally it was known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "generally"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean by "generally" is what is known that was implemented. That is, that it is important to prevent civilian casualties, civilian victims, that it is prohibited to prevent humanitarian aid from passing through, no matter which side it comes. Then what is important to save the wounded, whether they were regardless or whether they were civilians or military. So that's what I'm saying generally speaking, globally speaking, how to behave with prisoners, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the answer that you are giving, since we asked you about the corps and other officers, in your opinion what about other officers? Did they know it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Now I'd like us to -- no, there is one more question in relation to this, in relation to the knowledge. Do you know if the documents, specific documents in relation to Geneva Conventions, were given by the military hierarchy to the officers in question precisely on the level of the brigade? And if so, which ones? That is, technical documents and so on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the brigades in operation centre, in their operation centres, there were short excerpts from there, or that is, instructions, which were in relation to the humanitarian side of things, in relation to the Geneva Conventions. So the main duties of certain levels of command, and those who were involved in combat operations, what the positions were. That was specifically for prisoners and for wounded soldiers of the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you simply tell us -- I have seen you handle a piece of paper on your desk. Can you tell us, how was this summary technically made? I'm talking about the situation and the troops. Was there something that was very voluminous or was it something that was easy to handle and take around with you, in terms of the volume of the material of the documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The excerpt that could be -- that could fit onto one or two pages and give the most important instances, situations in relation to the conventions - now I cannot recall which exact items these were because I don't have the conventions before me or this kind of summary, this kind of memo - this is what it was: It was a kind of things to remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Now we can go on to another subject, and this is the subject that I'm interested in in relation to the crossing of the airport. The first question, generally put, may seem strange to you, but did it snow in Sarajevo; yes or no? In general. Generally speaking. And of course in wintertime.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first two winters that we spoke of, the first winter there was a lot of --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. I'm going to stop you. No. Just very simply. Does it snow in Sarajevo as a general rule; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, is it correct to say that if we have an environment which is covered in snow, particularly at night, the visibility is better if the snow reflects the light surrounding it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll withdraw the question. I will rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: So there's no misunderstanding, I object to all leading from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I take note of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked the following question yesterday, and I'm going to quote it as I can see it in my notes in English, therefore: [In English] "What did you expect your troops to do? What did you expect your troops to do if they were fired upon at night by one or more individuals from a group that may include civilians [Interpretation] or several individuals?" Just a minute. Just a minute. That was the question that you were asked yesterday by the Prosecution. First question: If at night fire is opened in wartime situation - so we are -- this is a hypothetical question we're talking about - and the soldier on whom the fire is opened, what can he think or what should he think about the type of the people who opened fire on him? Were they civilians or were they military? That is the first question. Did you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He can only think that he's being attacked; and therefore, he has to -- his duty to is defend himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So if he's defending himself in this situation with firing in response, whether discriminately or indiscriminately, at this level there is no importance at night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object to leading. My learned colleague has just -- my learned colleague has just put a specific proposition to the witness. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, putting a leading question to a witness and upon any objection to say "I'll put it in a different way" then the harm has been done. Would you please move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll go back to the question of orders that were transmitted. When an officer receives an order, what is he to do? This is a basic question, but I'd still like an answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has to read it, study it, to understand it. If there are certain things that are not clear, he has to address the superior command for clarifications, either general or specific, relating to specific parts. After that he has to compile an order for his own level, to whom he then addresses instructions, either orally or in written form, depending on the time. And in that order it is -- from that order of the superior command, he has to put in his order the elements of the order that are specifically relating to his unit, and he has to relate those contents that are directly connected to the conditions of -- conditions of the unit that is subordinate to him that will be used in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm going to go on to another subject which is not in relation to opening of fire but which is chronologically in relation to something that -- with the witness's testimony. I don't know whether I am allowed to do it, but I am going to do this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said yesterday in answering a question of the Prosecution that when people were crossing the runway, they were possibly bringing in ammunition. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, what type of ammunition was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume this was a different type of ammunition. Primarily ammunition for firing -- infantry ammunition that was possible to cross. I think it was in March 1993 that a vehicle was hit that was crossing the runway at night and that this vehicle exploded and the detonation lasted for some time, which meant that the airport runway, under the direct control of UNPROFOR representatives, explosive materials were carried. I think it was in Sarajevo or around Sarajevo. In Kotorac I believe this was, because -- from Donji Kotorac towards the sports airport that this ammunition was carried and that the explosive was needed to more speedily fortify this line. So there was ammunition that was carried and vehicles were used, then also explosive materials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This vehicle that exploded and that you say this vehicle probably carried explosive material, can you tell us what type of vehicle this was. Was this a civilian or a military vehicle? This is not a leading question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see it in the morning only. It was a lorry. But we could only see it when it was already burnt out, so you couldn't see what colour it had been, whether it had been a camouflage colour or whether it had been white, blue, or red. It could not be seen because the vehicle was destroyed because of the explosive materials that it was carrying. It was a military vehicle in any case because it was either mobilised or it had belonged to the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, if you were not able to at the time of the incident determine clearly to what category this vehicle belonged, were there any other factual circumstances that allowed you to come to the conclusion, the conclusion of your troops? And if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. This does not arise out of cross-examination. The cross-examination on the topic of vehicles was confined to cars and how the troops of the SRK according to the understanding of the witness would determine on appearance or other information the purpose of the vehicle, that is, military of civilian. This goes beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the questions of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I be heard, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm going to come back to the questions asked by the Prosecution in relation to private vehicles. But for the moment this witness gave quite a clear precise detailed answer from which we concluded that the incident had happened at night. And I believe that in relation to the question as to whether it was indiscriminate or discriminate fire, we have now new information, so it is now to find out how was it possible to assume or not assume in relation to the implementation of the conventions, and this is why this question is important to be asked of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I assume from those comments by my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. learned colleague that he's focussing on this incident of the vehicle that exploded on the runway. If that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If that's the case, this goes well beyond cross-examination. Cross-examination did not touch upon this particular incident. The witness has already said that effectively he's relying on hearsay, that as he understands it there is no indication as to the appearance of the vehicle before it was fired on, in any event, it was fired upon at night, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- But the vehicles in a more general way that were the subject of cross-examination. Would you please keep this in mind when you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, generally speaking, you were asked questions about vehicles that seemed to be civilian vehicles. And before I ask you the question that I was going to ask you, first I'll ask you another question: Do you know how was fuel controlled in the period of war in the part of the city of Sarajevo under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, I'm going to ask you a hypothetical question: Do you know -- I won't ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think we know what the hypothetical question is going to be. And it is inappropriate to be asked in re-examination of this witness. Again, the issue was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Ierace, I do not know what the hypothetical question is going to be. But keep in mind, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that if you ask a question which is inappropriate, then I might ask you to move to your next subject. Of course, it all depends on the question you're going to put to the witness. But please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Although, I am rather surprised by the apparent ability for the Prosecution to predict my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- No need to comment on that. I think I clearly expressed the Chamber waits for your question but at the same time it should be clear that the question should be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to the questions of vehicles, you said, I believe, that the other side had small lorries. I think you spoke of 2-tonne lorries, and pick-up trucks, and that they were used as weapons with mortars, so used them as mobile weapons. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, I don't recall that. I could be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please indication where you find this. And I will certainly assist you. I have got the computer version of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll go on to another subject, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you a question in relation to the archive which had been housed in barracks. We spoke about it yesterday. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The question that I'm asking you now in relation to the answer that you gave is the following: Apart from the Defence team, was there a person, no matter who it was, that you would have asked at any time in the 18 months that we're talking about any information and more specifically to find out if the documents belonging to the SRK were located in the Sokolac barracks; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can add something in relation to what I said yesterday. The archive, as far as I know, was not in the Sokolac barracks. I know that it had been prepared for Lukavica. I already said that, and I had taken part in some of the preparations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, witness. Please focus on the question. My question is the following: Apart from the Defence team, was there anyone else, anyone whosoever, who had asked you at any time if the SRK documents were located in the Sokolac barracks; yes or no? As far as you recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is a leading question. Again, I'm not assisted by the transcript from yesterday, but I recollect that I asked very broad questions of the witness to give him every opportunity to indicate any contact. And in my respectful submission, there is nothing arising out of that cross-examination that requires clarification of this type in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Mr. President, it seems there is an interpretation problem, I am told. In the content of the question, perhaps this is not how it came to the witness in Serbian, so I'd like to stress that we are only asking two things: If there was anyone else who had asked a question and if there is someone else, not counting the Defence team. Now, in relation to what Mr. Ierace said, I have to say that the questions that were asked by Mr. Ierace were in relation to some persons who were very well determined and whose name is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Directly arises from cross-examination. The Chamber would like to hear the answer to the question. Could you please answer the question, Mr. DP35, whether anyone else, during this period mentioned before, 18 months, ever asked you about the archives. So apart from members of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Organs of my command with the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a bit, because the interpreters have difficulties in translating what you say. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. So in this period, just like in the previous period, the organs of the command -- certain questions that were contentions, they could be linked to wartime. They addressed to me, because I was practically the only one who had been left of the officer cadre in the command of the current 5th Corps, and I was asked if I knew anything about the archive. Yesterday I answered that I had received the question by the representative of the Prosecution. I had received this question, but this was a general question, and I think that Milenko Radovic had been mentioned. I don't remember that man. Perhaps he had been together with the commander Andric. Somebody else -- a person, whether in civilian clothes or in uniform, who had been the representative of our military prosecutor's office, not from the Defence team, because the Defence team members did not enter the command because we met outside our command, and that they may have asked the question, these -- not the Defence. They didn't know anything about the archive. And my answer was that I knew what had happened until the moment when it was packed in Lukavica, because we had to move it. After the corps has been disbanded, I don't know any more. Perhaps parts of the archive had come to Sokolac or to Pale or to Trebinje or to Bijeljina. There was a unit in the war in Sokolac in the old part where we had temporary accommodation because there was a warehouse. Perhaps you should look there, whether it was archived there. I don't know what they did with it afterwards. Perhaps that representative of the military prosecutor's office may have found these document, because it seems to me that the document that was before me yesterday, this was the copy of the original document of the corps command, because there is a seal on it and there is a seal with the code of the station. So that's an original document. Whether this has been taken out of the packed -- of the pack of combat reports or whether it was just taken out or whether the whole parcel had come to this Tribunal, I don't know, because I was not there. That is the reason why my answer yesterday -- perhaps my answer wasn't very specific, but Radovic's surname is familiar with me. But to link up the first name and the last name as it was mentioned by the representative of the Prosecution, I don't know, because I don't know that man. I guarantee you, and people who know me, they know that I have a good memory and that from 1992 I can list you out of 200 names at least 100 names who were members of my unit. So I cannot state something which is not in my mind, and Radovic is not, so it is possible that some of the documents from the archive may have gotten to Sokolac and that's where they were found. I don't know whether it was the Defence team or the public prosecutor's office, whether they were involved in looking -- searching for those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question. If you said "they waited outside," where exactly was that? You said, "We met, and they waited outside. They did not enter." Where exactly was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about Sokolac. I'm talking specifically about the representative of the Defence, Pilipovic, when they came to Sokolac they told me -- she was there. She waited for me at the visitor's room. So if she had some notes, either to take or to ask me about them. That's what he said. So in any case she never came to me office. So she's here. So this can be confirmed or added to. But specifically, no interview with me was ever conducted in my office. That is, in the -- on the premises of the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you for this moment. When you met with members of the Defence team who waited outside in Sokolac, did you then enter that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I entered there after I finished talking with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What did you do in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I held the same duty during the war. I was the chief of AAD in the command of this corps. So I was chief of AAD in the command of the 5th Corps until the 5th of September, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the reason -- Sokolac was your office at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sokolac, the command of the 5th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which was -- your office was in the building and the members of the Defence team waited in the visitor's room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, some 50 metres, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Across the yard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was exactly the aim of that visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The aim of their visit was to tell -- to meet me, to ask me a certain number of questions which I could answer for the Defence team, or rather, before the Chamber in this case, because they knew that I was one of the officers who had stayed there and who was directly in the command and whose immediate superior was General Galic. So I did not call them. They learned it out of nowhere about me and they tried to establish contact with me, and I told them that I was at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the search for documents one of the specific issues discussed at that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. And even the search for documents was hardly mentioned. I was only asked whether I had any documents and which ones I did, and I said I did not know. Perhaps I still had a piece of paper. Because I simply had no conditions to keep any of these documents -- I mean, documents that I personally dealt with, that I simply did not have those documents. Subsequently I found the sketch, and you could see that it was only an annex, the sketch of the shelters at Mojmilo for actions against Lukavica. And I showed them. I believe it was in December, and I showed it to them and said, "Perhaps you can use this.." And here you have it, and I can explain that, because that was the diagram that existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you give any other documents that you -- or have you given any access to any other documents you retrieved later on at that same time to the Defence team, apart from the sketch you just mentioned on Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I didn't have any other documents. I saw documents, the map that you had at your disposal. But it came through other channels, not mine. But I know that I had used -- that I used it personally at the time, and I saw this map. I'm familiar with it and it has my handwriting on it in part, even though we took shifts with this. But I was not the one who gave it to the Defence and I did not have it at my disposal. It must have been taken from the archives somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, how much time would you still need to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I think not more than 15 minutes, if the witness gives us short answers. I have certain subjects to cover which I think can be done quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you're contemplating the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: There are two issues I'd like to raise relating in each case to queries I made of the Defence in court the other day. There's certain information which we're still waiting on from the Defence as to evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I expected a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That and a query in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a matter of hours rather than a matter of day, as far as I remember. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we discussed it yesterday in view of working hours that we finished last night and started this morning, I had no time to give it to my colleagues and I will do it today. Yesterday I was simply physically unable to write it down and send it. So I'll do it today after we finish our work. It will be around 15.00. I will send it to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The other issue involves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- The accused, Mr. President. If you recollect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do recollect that, and I take it it's not an issue to be dealt with at this moment. But I then take it that the Defence will have made up its mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We bear in mind this issue, and I think we shall also answer this question shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shortly -- by today or ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not think we shall be able to do it today in view of the pace of work here. I think that we shall discuss it not in the Tribunal but when we go to visit General Galic, and I presume it will be on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there would be an opportunity to -- if there's any need, to discuss or comment on the position the Defence takes by next Monday. Would that be -- I do understand -- I do appreciate that we can't expect the Defence to give the information requested unless there has been a proper occasion to discuss the matter with the accused. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And perhaps if a deadline could be set of Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I expect that if the discussions have taken place on Friday in the afternoon, that the decision could be reached during the weekend so that the Prosecution is informed by next Monday morning. We are sitting in the afternoon next week. Yes. Then we'll adjourn until ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Over the break I've looked at the transcript from yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- In relation to the topic of archival material and contact with the Defence. I seek leave to ask further questions following the conclusion of re-examination on that topic. The basis for the application is that the witness has said that since he gave his evidence yesterday, he now recalls further matters. And on the face of it, there appear to be some contradictions between his evidence given today on that topic and his evidence given yesterday. I seek to explore those differences and this further information that he's provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber understands your application to refer to the matters you tried to explore more deeply in cross-examination, not new areas to be explored, unless it directly results from answers given to where you got no answers yesterday. To that extent, the Chamber will grant the application. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. As you examined this witness in great detail on this point, we'd really like not to waste too much time with this, apart from the matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like us to go back to what you said regarding the AAD weapons, arising from questions asked of you by the Prosecution. And on the basis of a proposal of the Prosecution, you were asked to put on the map numbers for some positions and then the command post and forward command post, and it turned out that you could not mark everything on this map for technical reasons, I believe. Now, will you please tell us, what are these reasons in a nutshell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The forward command post at Nisici there is no -- the upper part of the map, so I put an arrow there, and it was at a distance of some 20 to 25 kilometres north-north-west of Vogosca. Cemerska forward command post, once again outside the map, below Lukavica -- Rakovica, it's on the road towards Kjevoto [phoen] -- Trnovo, and that is some 15 to 20 kilometres south of the end of the map, and that is why I couldn't draw that. And the same applies to firing positions of AAD brigades in the area of Ilijas and part of the Igman brigade, that is, Blazuj, Rakovica. On Rakovica I did mark a certain position. So these are minor imprecisions which I could not draw on the map because they are outside the map, but I think that provided you with other information concerning the weaponry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Concerning the number of pieces - and by this I mean the information at the corps level - what can you tell us about two things, that is: First, the deployment of these pieces, not immediately in the vicinity of Sarajevo but on the front? And I'm referring to the SRK. And on the other hand, did you know how long was the front line in kilometres that would concern the SRK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, the length of the front line on this -- I will start from here. The length of the front line, as far as I can remember - but I don't think I will go off the mark too much - was about 50 kilometres, and it had two lines, the front one and the rear one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is very important to rectify, because I think that the figure -- the figure that was mentioned in the English transcript is not what I heard. I think we are talking about a bigger -- about a longer front line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you slowly repeat how long was the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you think there might be some misunderstanding, you should not explain that it was longer but just ask the witness again in order to avoid whatever confusion to repeat his answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I should be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, will you please tell us once again how long was the front. But be -- speak slowly so -- because -- so that everybody can hear what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was over 250 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. And now you can resume your explanation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The front line -- there were two types of front line, one -- we call them rings. There was an inner ring, and that was the front line facing Sarajevo. And there was also an outer ring, which was behind our backs, as we said it. It was towards Gorazde, towards other parts of the front, towards Cemerska Mount and so on. So we had two front lines. Within the area of responsibility, we had AAD units. And basically they were to be between a kilometre or perhaps more, depending on the deployment of defence troops in the depth of the front. But it so happened that some of our positions had to remain on the first front line, as, for instance, in the sports air field, and they were -- they had been positions before the start of combat operations and their intention was to defend the Butmir air field. However, this air field was not in our area of responsibility, and we kept those positions and performed other combat tasks from there. Secondly, the positions of the units. I had a lot of difficulty in establishing the conventional positions for the AAD because during those three years that we're talking about, there were practically no actions from the air, so that the positions were frequently fragmented. And what I drew on the map was our basic firing positions.
