That is, I could not draw the position of a piece which according to -- under the technical principles was outside the area where we kept the firing position. In those parts of the map where I drew their positions do not show the full deployment of the Ilijas -- of AAD pieces in the Ilijas Brigade, and they had a circular deployment towards Visoko, towards Cemerska Mount, et cetera. On the map shown by the Defence from Nisici, which shows also part of the Nisici plateau, shows the deployment with marked positions or pieces which were groups. On the Nisici plateau, there wasn't a special AAD unit. But from the corps and brigade AAD units, one or two pieces were taken from them to set up the AAD on the Nisici plateau and the same held true on the Trnovo axis, and that is not marked on the map. I believe I've given you enough information about the method of deployment and possibilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you to be so kind as to answer the following question: The number of weapons that you indicated yesterday - I will not repeat it - but you told us we had so many such weapons and so on. So my question is: Does it also hold true of other positions, other than the positions which could be marked on the map that you used? In other words, were there also weapons outside this limited area shown on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the number of pieces in the whole area, which means that I also included those parts which I could not show on the map, and this is the Nisici plateau, the Ilijas Brigade, and the Trnovo area. I gave the number of pieces as per calibre. I was not asked about weapons of the 40-millimetre calibre and, one, the so-called Bofors, and there were 42 of them in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Witness, I'm changing the subject, and it will be my last subject. We spoke about missions of sending the ammunition into the city. And so my question is: How would you qualify these missions of delivery of ammunition into the part of the city which remained under the control of the BH forces, in terms of degree? Were there major deliveries for the adversary, or how would you describe them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my assessment - and it's not only mine, it is something that we arrived at at discussions and analysis on the basis of information that we had - is that those were important quantities of equipment, especially in the period of interest to us. Later on it must have changed because...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please do go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. I thought you were interrupting me. Later on - I don't know when exactly - so-called rapid intervention forces were set up, and they helped significantly the adversary forces. So through the tunnel across the airport runway and using some other corridors we could also see that some of it went through the area at Ilidza. A vehicle was stopped with a double bottom, and at the bottom there were some explosive devices and combat devices, so that it was even delivered through our area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. My question is as follows: Speaking from the strategic point of view, were these deliveries important, these missions? Were they important or not? Strategically speaking. I'm speaking from the point of view of logistics and strategy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logistically speaking, yes, of course. They were important. Now strategically, it is more difficult to say. But strategically speaking, inevitably, yes, and from this operational point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I will ask you something -- a theoretical question: If soldiers had to carry out important logistic missions, and if they are on the point of being discovered, for instance, when crossing the runway, say, under the cover of darkness, what would have been their military reaction if they had been discovered there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the soldiers of the opposite side, of the adversary?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object. Mr. President. This didn't arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perfectly, it does arise directly, because the question was as follows: Mr. Ierace was asking whether this was happening under cover of darkness. Don't you think that the last thing they would do would be to open the fire, because that would then reveal their positions? Now my question is to know -- I believe this was quite vital with regard to this particular itinerary, to this particular route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The subject is permissible, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Nevertheless, would you please rephrase your question, because there are some elements in it which are really difficult to understand from a practical point of view. I am especially pointing at the part "at the point of being." How would you translate that in rather factual terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now, I'd like to turn now to the adversary troops when they were transporting weapon, that is, ammunition, across the runway, and under cover of the night. If these soldiers - this is a hypothetical question - if these soldiers know that they are on the point of being seen possibly, that is, discovered, and that perhaps they were able to see for themselves some worrying movements, what would have been their response strictly militarily speaking? What do you think about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, they were carrying out a combat task. I rule out -- and I believe that you need not ask whether among them there were also civilians. I've already said, they were carrying out a combat, a military task, in any case. Whether fire was open or not - and this is primarily about opening -- whether our fire was open in response to their opening of fire - it did happen. It did occur that fire was opened in order to turn the attention away from one point on the runway, in order to make the other part of the runway safer. So this was manoeuvring fire. In order to divert attention of our forces that were able to fire, in order to open fire on one part and not on the other. Another detail: We are convinced that crossing the runway was done under the umbrella of the UN forces. This even happened during daytime. And that's why we -- in those situations we protested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the very last question: You said something in your answer regarding manoeuvring fire. Can you tell us, do you know what is diversionary fire? This is diversionary fire.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there is a manoeuvre to be done by movement and fire. Manoeuvring by fire, so it's either to divert attention or to prevent an attack. There is a manoeuvre tactical act, action. In order to conduct movement in one part, in order to draw out the forces of the opponent, while the actual main attack would happen in a different direction. So this is how this type of fire works, on a different type of runway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question: What can you tell us about the frequency of such diversionary fire on the runway?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's very hard to say. Sometimes it would happen in two or three days twice or sometimes in -- within ten days it would happen twice, or perhaps it happened twice during one single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm just going to check the transcript. I believe we have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, you asked permission to put some additional questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are allowed to do so now. Further cross-examination by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, earlier this morning you were asked some questions about who, if anyone, you had spoken to on the topic of access to archival material, and you said, "I can add something in relation to what I said yesterday." Did you recollect further material overnight on this topic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't able to, apart that I had said that I had given a sketch from Mojmilo as additional, because I found it coincidentally during the time I was waiting to come and testify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said this morning that you met at Sokolac with some people, including a representative of your military prosecutor's office. When did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps a year ago. I was called -- I was summoned to see General Andric, and he asked me whether I knew something, and there was a civilian present there and some of our other senior officers. He asked me if I knew anything. And while I was thinking about it, I gave some additional information because my answer was that I did not know of the location where the archive may have been put and that it was possible that one part of it was in Sokolac. So that was my explanation in relation to what I had said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me be clear on, firstly, those details. You were at Sokolac barracks at that stage when you received the call from the military prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that is not the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You said you were called -- you were summoned to see General Andric, and he asked whether you knew something. Where were you when you were summoned? Where were you exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in my office on the same floor in the corps command where General Andric was. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you walked up the corridor to his office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you entered his office, how many other people were there with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were two of his assistants, his close associates, and one civilian. He was not introduced to me. Maybe he was and I've forgotten it, but I heard from the others or I may have understood from the others that the others told me that this other person was somebody from the military prosecutor's office. That's why I don't remember the name. Because I don't know many people from those structures, from those institutions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that he asked -- well, do you say that the general asked you if you knew where the archive was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with all due respect, I have to object to the way that the questions are phrased. Asking a question of a witness -- asking if he was -- he had used a corridor, a specific corridor. Can we just focus this type of questioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think you opposed against the way Mr. Ierace presented the earlier testimony, and I think Mr. Ierace tried to avoid whatever misunderstanding in this respect. Let's try to be as efficient as possible. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told him that you did not know the location but you suggested that it may be -- or part of it may be in Sokolac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I presumed that it may be there. It may have happened to go there together with the files of the logistics base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were in Sokolac when you had that conversation, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you told him that it may be in Sokolac, did you mean in the same complex where you and he were talking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far from where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a different building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a different building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did you take him to that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said already. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you tell him where in that building he should look?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell him the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in the building where the units of the logistics department were during the war, and that they may have put the documents there. During the move a part of the archive may have gotten there, but I did not enter the premises. And in that old building where these units may have filed their archive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, was there anything else discussed apart from that topic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then leave his office?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a representative of the Defence, Pilipovic, did you mean Madam Pilipovic who is seated to your left at the moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned that she waited for you at the visitor's room. Was that the same day that you were having the conversation with the general, General Andric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was that before or after the conversation with General Andric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I met Ms. Pilipovic before this conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Why were you referring to a particular occasion where Madam Pilipovic was waiting for you in the visitor's room? What was the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which occasion?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said this morning -- you were asked by Mr. President, "If you said 'they waited outside' where exactly was that?" You said "we met and they waited outside. They did not enter." "Where exactly was that"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said, "I'm talking about Sokolac. I'm talking specifically about the representative of the Defence, Pilipovic. When they came to Sokolac, she was there. She waited for me at the visitor's room."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the significance of that meeting in relation to this topic of the archival material? Why did you mention it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention the link between the archive and Ms. Pilipovic. I mentioned the discussions, because you had asked me whether there were conversations regarding the archive. So I had separated the conversation took place at General Andric's in relation to the archive and the discussions which were in relation to my participation in this process, in the Defence case, which was separate. It was mostly without any documents that I spoke to them, mostly, without any documents at my disposal. That's how I talked to Ms. Pilipovic, not the documents, not with the documents that I had in front of me. I'd already stressed this in my previous answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, to be clear on this, did Madam Pilipovic or anyone else from the Defence ask you any questions at all about where any of the archival material for the SRK could be located?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be good to specify the time, because earlier we had asked some questions. It will be good to specify the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I to understand this question to be about this meeting or in general, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In general. Did the members of the Defence, including Madam Pilipovic, have ever asked you any question about where any of the archival material for the SRK could be located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether they asked such questions. Why do I say this? I'm saying this because I had said that I did not have at my disposal some documents that would have made it easier, that would have made it easier for me to participate in the defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tell us that you don't remember whether they asked such questions. Is it your evidence that whether they asked such questions or not, you did not take them to any archival material, apart from the sketch that you've told us about? And that was in your possession, in any event. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I found it later by chance among other documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- From. Now, you said this morning that you had taken some part in some of the preparations. And I take that to be reference to the preparations of the archival material. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, "I know that it had been prepared for Lukavica." What do you mean by saying --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At Lukavica. When did you take part in some of those preparations of the archival material?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The material for the archive was prepared in the course of 1995 for all the previous years, and I took part in this as a member of the team in compiling them, putting them together, preparing them for being archived. Following the signing of the Dayton Agreement and the decision that we should move out together with the command, I knew where the materials were, and those members of the team that had worked with me on this previously, they had a key at their disposal and this material was to be packed, transported, and put away. Whether it was taken to Pale or to some other location, I do not know. I mentioned yesterday or the day before yesterday my answer, because at that time I was in the field. I was involved in the movement of weapons and equipment of the AAD together with the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please stop. Who were the members of the team that worked with you on the packing of the archival material? You mentioned they had a key at their disposal. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This no longer stems from the cross-examination or from the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll allow the witness to answer this question and then -- Could you tell us who were the members of the team with whom you did the packing of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The members of the team were from the temporary composition. I wouldn't -- I would rather not name them. These were two civilians, members of our unit, a civilian, and a typist who was making a list and notes. They were just able to move -- transport the documents to some location because very soon afterwards there was the disbanding of the corps. Now, what happened to the materials following the disbanding of the corps, I don't know, because I remained in the vicinity of Sokolac together with all the technical equipment and materiel under a tent and I was not able to keep with me any part of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that what remained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, the question was the names of those that were in the team. You said you would rather not mention their names. We'll now turn into private session so that you can give us those names without the outside of the world to hear the answers you are giving. One moment, please. Could we turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday I asked you this question: "Following Dayton, did you have anything at all directly or indirectly to do with moving any of the archival material of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps at any stage after December 1995?" And you replied, in part -- this is the commencement of your answer: "After December 1995, I know that the archival material was moved to Pale," and you went on to say that you were at Sokolac and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- After that. A few minutes ago you said, "Whether it was taken to Pale or some other location, I don't know."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Yesterday you said, "After December 1995, I know that the archival material was moved to Pale." And today you say you don't know if it went to Pale.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with yesterday's phrasing. I don't know -- yesterday I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Yesterday, according to the transcript, you said, "After December 1995, I know that the archival material was moved to Pale. But at the time I was withdrawing anti-aircraft equipment from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps area and the Sokolac region, and I no longer had access to that archival material and I can't tell you what happened to it later on." That's your words as they were written down yesterday. Mr. Ierace, you asked -- And Mr. Ierace now asked you why you said yesterday that the archives were transported to Pale, whereas you say today that you didn't know whether they went to Pale or to -- you mentioned a few other places. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The word "I know," I cannot Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. confirm that I'd said it yesterday, and I'm linking yesterday's answer and today's answer, which has the same meaning, but there is this word "know" or "not know" which makes it be the complete opposite of each other. If I had said that I was in Sokolac for taking out the material, then this word of mine, "I know" transcribed yesterday it could be rather hasty, because I could not have followed the archives to Pale for me to say "I know." I could have said "I know that it was supposed to go to Pale," if you'll allow me to add this to my answer -- I know that this was supposed to go to Pale, and that would have been identical with the meaning of what was said today. I do not wish in any way to prevent you from finding out anything, but I don't want to say or be seen to be saying something yesterday and something else today. I could not have followed its movement to Pale if I was in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I believe that if we undertake a complete reading of what the witness said yesterday, I think a little bit of the situation could be clarified. This is what I'm allowing myself to do. Specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could please draw the attention to those keywords so that we can read them on our computers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In such a way it does not give a clue to the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The keyword is, if I can find it, [In English] "Access" by example or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is lines 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll repeat it. I stopped halfway the answer. You also said, "And I no longer had access to that archival material, and I can't tell you what happened to it later on." Does that make you feel that you should add something to your answer or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only to confirm that I know it went to Pale. It should be added "I know", that it should have gone to Pale, that it was supposed to go to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This morning you said, "After the corps has been disbanded, I don't know any more." When exactly was the 4th Corps -- the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, I should say, disbanded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: February -- February 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that you say it was moved, whether to Pale or somewhere else from Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: December 1995/January 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this question was already asked and already answered, and the witness said "after December 1995." There are some questions which are being asked again which have been already clearly answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say the others had a key to the archive, was it a key to a locked truck, a key to a trunk, a key to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has already answered, because he spoke about the key to the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least, what I believe I heard in his language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The key to the office, practically. And I even think that it wasn't in the hands of the members of the team but that it was Colonel Zarkovic who had it, who remained in that building with some men who were to organise the move. And we went after our own business.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In view of that answer, Mr. President, one further question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your reference to Colonel Zarkovic, is that Colonel Zarkovic who was a senior officer of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In the English transcript, the key is not related to a building, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. But if there's any need to check that in the original tape, the Chamber will assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, the Judges have several questions for you as well. The first questions will be put to you by Judge Nieto-Navia. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Could the map be shown to the witness. I would like to see the airport area, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The map should be moved a bit downwards. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that you said that the positions X1 and X5, as far as I can see, were not able to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4 and 5. It is 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, I cannot see that very well -- 4 and 5 were not able to fire towards the runway of the airport. Was that your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You said that there were other units which could do so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Could you point to the -- those units, to the place where those units were.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Infantry units, Dobrinja I; infantry units, Novakovici houses, part of Donji Kotorac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Were those units under your command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Do you know whether those units ever opened fire towards the runway of the airport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an exact answer, but they did open it. That was not under any jurisdiction and under my immediate control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: But how do you know that they did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the -- the command post is in the immediate vicinity. You can see it to the right. And in the building, in the command building in Lukavica - and it says "KM" - I was frequently at positions X4, 5, and 6. And from the position X6, one could follow exactly where the circle is placed next to "X6." In this circle is an elevation from which one couldn't open fire but one could not -- but one could observe. And that is why I related the observation post to this order to open or not open fire in the direction of the runway.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I noticed that the witness was pointing to the screen. I wonder if he could be directed to point at the map on the ELMO so that we can follow those positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes. But he mentioned X6, yes, the command post.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was pointing at X6. No, the command -- I mentioned the command in Lukavica and the observation post was at X6, and I'm pointing at it now. KM, which is the command post Lukavica, then positions in Dobrinja, Donji Kotorac, and the observation post at X6, that is what I showed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Did you ever personally observe those units when they were opening fire towards the runway?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say I saw it with my own eyes, because from the position of contact at Dobrinja I and Dobrinja IV, towards Dobrinja II and III, one could hear fire from there all the time, and it was the immediate interface, because there wasn't a street separating the forces, and it would be frequently only walls in one building. One could hear fire frequently from there, and it was very difficult to say whether fire was being opened in the direction of the runway or whether fighting was going on in some part of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you personally didn't see those units firing towards the runway. That's your testimony.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: But you know -- you know that those units opened fire sometime, because you heard that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And after all, it was their job to follow, to keep under eye this part of the runway because that was within their lines, within their combat assignment lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Do you know which part of the runway was used, if it was used, for crossing of the BiH units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really say exactly, but I don't think it was the first third or perhaps first quarter of it. But, rather, the part which was further away, towards this area where Muslim forces were deployed. So from here it is only -- only this part was in our area of responsibility, this area which I am pointing at now. So down -- I would say it was rather down the runway in this direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Do you mean to the west-north-western part of the airport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the north-western part. That is, in the direction of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Now I will move to another topic. Were you trained by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Was part of your training some information on the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: What do you mean by "in part"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I graduated from the academy in 1972, so in part. The decisions of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and the definitions in the additional protocols and those which had to do with the United Nations and all the rest. That is why I say yes, but insofar as we could at that time, between 1968 and 1972, yes, from what we could learn and remember. And we remembered what one does not need to learn, something that one remembers by simply knowing what international relations are in other aspects, from conversations, from the media, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Do you know whether after 1962 up until 1992 the soldiers were trained or received lessons on the Geneva Conventions? I don't mean the officers but the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were individual questions, just as there were through the civil defence the population was given booklets with instructions how to -- what kind of conduct they should apply in their own defence in case of the extension of first aid, in case of capture, and so forth. So they were excerpts of general nature that were distributed among the population and among the soldiers as well, elementary matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I have another question: Is the fire, the anti-aircraft fire, a direct or indirect fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Direct only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions to you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to ask you if you can tell me what was roughly the percentage of former JNA members amongst your troops, approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All unit members had served their military service with the JNA before the war. But in the units of the permanent JNA forces until January 1992, those men who were in my unit, in my regiment, the regiment I commanded from July 1992, in my unit there were four officers - active-duty, I mean. I was the fifth such officer, and I also had - but I may go wrong - 15 soldiers under contract, and I also had two civilians, that is, people who were in the former unit in the JNA. That's it. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Perhaps you should make my question clearer. If I understand you well, you testified that during the military service, one learnt the ABC's of humanitarian law, that is, the Geneva Conventions. So my question has to do with those people who were trained, that is, those who did their military service with the JNA and who then are supposed to have received some elementary instruction in humanitarian law. So my question was about the number -- about the percentage, the share of such men amongst your troops. If I understand you well, you tell us that everybody did his military service, so in other words you could say that all the men under your command and in the corps, too, had done their military service and, therefore, were also aware more or less with the general principles of the Geneva Conventions. Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said. Some elementary, that is, the minimum knowledge. Yes, they had that. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Right. Then I'm going to broach another subject, if I may. If I understand you well, the positions exist in order to pursue a particular military objective. Can you briefly explain to us the military reason behind the choice of how your troops would be deployed around the city of Sarajevo. What was the objective -- the military objective you pursued? Because you said that the other party did not have any air force. And therefore, what was it that you pursued and the decision to -- your decision or the decision of a corps to deploy the troops at the positions that you chose was part of which plan, whether such decisions were taken by you or at the corps level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my earlier explanations of the positions, I already said that when I arrived there in July 1992, that at that time, that July, had already those covered assignments. I'm talking about regiment units. And that this combat assignment was not significantly changed during the period of time we are talking about here. So my predecessors whom I did not find there when I got to the regiment, because they had left for various reasons, by that time, before the conflict broke out, that is, before April, they had already defined those firing positions, because whenever there was a certain tension in a country or around it, then the anti-aircraft defence units are the first ones to reach their combat positions. And even in peacetime, whilst they were still a part of the JNA, they already had certain firing positions which they took in order to defend certain facilities or certain directions. My units from the beginning, that is, from 1992 -- that is, in 1992 they took those positions in order to enable the mobilisation and further activities arising from the combat assignments of the corps. The sports air field was taken in March, as far as I learnt from those men whom I found there. And as such, in the Yugoslav People's Army, it was -- served as a training ground and also for -- and it was used as a facility, as a tactical, as an immobile object for training. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, perhaps I did not phrase my question precisely. And I would also like to seek a clarification. You said that you inherited those positions, that is, that the positions had already been taken and defined before you came there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Therefore, you were aware -- you were familiar with a military plan, that is, these positions were taken based on a particular military objective that was pursued on the basis of a plan. So my question is: Can you briefly explain to us the why. Why did the military choose those positions? Secondly, did the objective pursuit remain the same for the duration of the conflict? And that is my question. Or did it change? And will you please try to be as precise as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. possible and not -- and in just so many words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a nutshell, the plan of deployment of the units in my regiment, which existed during the JNA time, did not exist any longer and was not of use to us because it had lost the importance. It applied to some completely different tasks because the territory which the regiment could use and move about had changed completely. The JNA troops prior to the war had a completely different area than the Sarajevo Corps, so the peacetime plan could not be used in wartime. The units happened to be on the positions that they were at and from those positions -- at those positions they carried out preparations for air combat, which started only three years later. And from those positions, with of course the necessary shifts, they also provided support to units at this or some other parts of the front in Sarajevo. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Right. So you shifted some positions, didn't you, depending on the military needs within the framework of a plan? Now, the purpose, the objective, the orders that were given you, the objective that you pursued, was what, briefly speaking? You were responsible for what, to do what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why, I was responsible for the preparation of the orders and preparation of a proposal to say whether one could extend support and provide anti-aircraft defence from the existing positions or whether a certain shift, a certain move was needed, whether the positions ought to have been changed. And the pieces can be moved within a particular existing position. They can be put closer together or perhaps a platoon of the battery -- a battery has two platoons. So the platoon can be moved or the whole battery can be moved. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. I shall move to another subject. That will be the last one. You said with regard to the fire which would last -- fire from different weapons, which would last for a few moments - and I quote you in English - [In English] "But now I cannot associate that event with any special importance." [Interpretation] So my question is -- I'd like to understand exactly what you said, so I'm asking you to clarify. What did you mean by the phrase "it can ring a bell"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could you just remind me what is it that we were talking about. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] It was a Prosecutor's question, and the Prosecutor asked you about a shot sometime towards the end of the year, around Christmas 1992, and it happened -- that is, there were several shots fired during 20 minutes or so. 20 minutes came up. But during a period of time. And to this question your answer was, and I quote, [In English] "But now I cannot associate that event with any special importance." [Interpretation] Do you remember it now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And do you remember the question too, witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. I understand now. There was some slight confusion about the term and the dates. We were talking about Christmas, and then we talked whether it was the Orthodox Christmas or the Catholic Christmas, was I in Mostar, or in Sarajevo, and I said that I was in Trebevic. The Prosecution said that the fire lasted 20 minutes? I do not recall that. That is what I'm saying. But perhaps my memory would have been jogged if I knew specifically. And then a member of the Prosecutor's team -- JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] No, no, no. It does not matter whether it was 20 minutes or 15 or 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you said that there was also 40-millimetre fire. And I tried to answer, because if I put together those event, nobody -- because I was interrupted then. So I must say that this battery with -- that is, this platoon with 40-millimetre pieces was nearest to me. But nobody lodged a protest with me. Nobody protested against this fire being open from 40-millimetre pieces which were part of the regiment artillery, and there were such Bofors, that is, 40-millimetre. There were also in other places in -- they were with the brigade units which were not under my jurisdiction directly, which were part of brigades, and they could have opened fire. This does not mean that I am trying to shift the responsibility, that it is something that escaped my control, that fire -- that 40-millimetre fire had been -- was opened without my authorisation. But I also said when we were talking about the military hospital that 40-millimetre fire, if it was a Christmas fire, that it could only mean random wanton fire, but it could not produce any effect -- that it could not affect or hit the military hospital from the position at Vrace. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please repeat for the interpreters because they did not hear your answer. Witness, the end of your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The end of the answer or the whole answer? JUDGE EL MAHDI: No, no, no. Just the last sentence, because the interpreter lost it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My last sentence. I see. If fire was opened from the Vrace positions towards the military hospital - and this has already been mentioned - and I said that if fire was opened without my authorisation but then it must have been just wanton arbitrary fire which would produce no effect on the military hospital or any other target. It means that it could not destroy troops. If it hit the wall of any building which was in its way, then it could have. But I wasn't asked that and I didn't explain it. Then it will be damage of the wall of about this size and depth of about 2 or 3 fingers, that is, not even -- so that bullet would not have even damaged the brick. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And tell us, why hit the wall without hitting the troops, without producing casualties? Can you please explain it to me in two words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if it was just arbitrary fire, somebody was firing random shots to mark a particular holiday, such as Easter or Christmas or the new year, just fires like that. Another objective would be a support to show that there were units there. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Well, this is what I do not understand, because I'm not getting the interpretation. There seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- Is -- I'll try to speak some English words and see --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I'm creating the problem. Is the French translation functioning now? Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I gave the explanation. Do I have to repeat it now because of the interpretation problems? JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. Because I didn't follow you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You asked what was the objective of opening fire. If, as I said, if the fire was opened without an order, without the authorisation to do so, without any report -- as commander of the regiment, that means that the fire was opened as wanton and arbitrary firing. And this is a Balkan habit, a custom. I don't know what it's like in other countries. But that means that for New Year, for Christmas, fire is opened. That happens in peacetime too. That's what it was. However, this fire may have only occurred for a very short time because they received ammunition which was in the central warehouse. And I headed the disposal of my unit in coffee spoons, so to speak, so they had to report what they were using it for and we had to report what they were using it for. But if there was some action that was planned, some operation that was planned, as it was alleged that it lasted for 20 minutes, then I would have had to know about this order and I never knew about this kind of order because there would be no purpose in firing this at night. For 20 minutes in order to waste ammunition. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have some questions for you as well, but since that will take certainly more than two or three minutes, we'll first have a break and we'll adjourn until five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. DP35, I've got a few questions for you as well. You told us that from your Vrace positions the state hospital could not be targeted. What -- how many storeys does the main building of the state hospital have, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven or eight, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it a high-rise building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a high-rise building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could it be seen from Vrace, the upper part of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps the roof part of the upper-most storey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I never -- I did come to that position, but it was never from that position that we were looking at what was in front of us and what was the top floor of the hospital. We never discussed about the position of the military hospital. I know that we had the data that there were in some other parts that there were weapons or some ammunition, that in some parts where this was -- some targets where this was done, but we couldn't reach them. So we would take weapons and ammunition to other positions so that they could target those other targets from other positions, but we never -- it was never within our range to target those other parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- but the higher parts were in the range that you could target or not? It's not entirely clear to me what you tell us about -- if you tell me -- let me put the question a different way to you. If you tell me that you might have been able to see the upper part of the building, why could you not have targeted that part of the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I can't be sure whether the top part could be seen, the top part of the hospital. I also said that the hospital -- it was not in our interest for our units to target it. It wasn't a target we would target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether you did it but whether you could have done it, technically.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically, what I said in the first part of my answer, it is probable that the top parts could have been targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is that you said this morning that you ruled out that among those crossing the runway, there were civilians. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you understood me correctly. I ruled it out because I was not in a position to see whether these civilians were parts of these groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say, "I didn't know. It was not impossible."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question is -- I tried to get a better understanding of your testimony in respect of what I will call Christmas fire. That means firing of weaponry at an occasion such as Christmas, and I'd like to concentrate on the 24th of December, when you said you were at Trebevic. You testified that no warning was given to you and that the firing was not upon your orders. This suggests that you knew about such an event but that you had received no previous warning and that you did not order to participate in such fire. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd like to clarify the first part. I didn't know, but I found out when we were speaking about Christmas from the Prosecution -- I found out that this was opening of fire on Christmas. But this was the Catholic Christmas. If you're speaking about the 25th of December, I did not know about it. I did not know about the opening of fire. Now, if I'm saying if there was an opening of fire, I did not have an order for some members of my unit to take -- some parts of my unit to take part in that. I can just add something else: If it's Christmas, then it's a Catholic Christmas, and no unit of mine had any purpose of opening -- firing wantonly or opening fire, because in the parts of Sarajevo towards Vrace, there were no Croats, and there would be -- and there was no HVO units in that part of Sarajevo that was turned towards us. So if there was any opening of fire, that was without my authority, outside of my control. But I did not receive any protest, any criticism, any remark in relation to this opening of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand you. You did not receive any protest. We heard evidence that intensive random fire was -- took place on the 24th of December, when you said you were in Trebevic. On the one hand side, your testimony does not exclude for the possibility that intensive random fire -- I'm not talking about hitting objects, but fire as you described it yourself, random shots, took place -- you do not exclude for that and you told us that on the 24th of December, you were in Trebevic. Could you -- if you do not exclude for it, would you agree with me that if such an event would have happened, that you would have heard it, being on Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have happened. I would have been able to hear that, but the question is whether I can't remember. But I really -- it doesn't stand out in my mind that there was such opening of fire on such a date. That is not in my recollection. I really don't know whether on the occasion of any holiday I said that wanton opening of fire was possible but whether on any such holiday, Catholic or Orthodox or Muslim holiday, whether we were prevented from opening fire. I know that for New Year, my task was to inspect the units and to make sure that and to warn the units not to open fire, precisely not to provoke and to cause disorder because somebody was marking such a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have no recollection, you say. Do I have to understand this that you do not exclude it but you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is about complaints. You were asked how General Galic would deal with complaints about shelling. The question was whether he dealt with it in a professional way, and you answered that he would not just have a glance at such protests but would deal with it seriously. That's how I understood your answer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The questions were about complaints about shelling. Would -- did General Galic, if there were any complaints about sniping, deal with it similarly seriously as the way you told us he dealt with complaints about shelling? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence must object to this in the current --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if there's any problem of translation, whatever, but if the other party puts a question to -- if it's a technical matter, fine. If it goes to the content of the question, I would first ask the witness to answer the question unless --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The content of the question, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we first -- could I ask the usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, as a general rule, the parties are supposed not to intervene apart from matters like there's no translation or something like that on questions from the Bench. Nevertheless, since the Chamber is aware that this is a sensitive issue, that we'll give you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. an opportunity to express yourself, but that's an exception to the rule. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My objection is in that I carefully followed in the last two days the testimony of Witness DP35, and in his answers he never said that he received protests in relation to sniper incidents. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the reason why I asked -- why we would deal with it in a similar way if there had been any. So it was not included in the question that there were. So if that would be your objection, then...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, he said that he never received protests, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness did not receive any protests, yes. But I was not asking about protests addressed to the witness. I was asking about the way the accused was dealing with protests, whether the witness knew anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is -- the Chamber has decided that the objection is denied. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. DP35, I asked you a question. Do you still remember my question? The question was about the way the -- General Galic would deal with any protests about sniping if there were any. Could you please answer the question, whether it was in a similar way or different. Please proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assessment is, although I couldn't attend the way or couldn't be present directly how the general dealt with that, but I believe that the approach to any protest was the same, was equitable, and I believe that this is how it was done. But as far as the sniping itself, I know very little, and I couldn't really comment further on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking about your personal knowledge of the sniping but whether you were ever -- whether you ever heard how General Galic would deal with complaints about sniping.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said in the beginning that my assessment was that it was the same approach to those protests and for other protests. So for those protests and the protests which were -- had different content.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On what is your assessment based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I said I couldn't be directly present there when a protest was discussed, because I couldn't be present. If a protest was discussed at a meeting where other members of the command staff attended, then I could have followed that. But if a protest was discussed outside this meeting, then General Galic must have discussed this through his liaison officer through whom the protests went and with possibly some people whose task was to study this and assess it. So that's why my assessment is that the approach of General Galic was the same for all protests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand you correctly if you say that protests about sniping were not the subject of even mentioning during the meetings you attended? Were they mentioned? Were they discussed? Were they not mentioned? Were they ...?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mentioned, as well as other protests, if they occurred prior to the meeting. If these protests occurred after the meeting and then they were resolved in the period of one day, say, of one working day, or in the course of the daytime, then it must have been discussed with other people outside the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at those occasions where these protests about sniping were mentioned during the meeting, what would be said about it? What would be the procedure to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a warning that was given to the relevant persons who would forward that warning and check it in the units whether fire was opened, for instance. Or there was a warning -- that was the task given to the liaison officer with UNPROFOR to check whether the protest was based on facts, on something that had really happened. And we always stressed that there were many protests that occurred which were not based factually and that practically people were just involved in studying this, discussing it, and then the opposite thing was true. And there were other -- firing was also discussed in relation to the weapons which need not have had optical sights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there ever given an instruction to investigate at your side - that means the Bosnian Serb forces - to investigate the complaint as to the facts underlying the complaint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commissions were set up, teams, to check the information. But now I cannot really tell you how many of them, where, and in relation to what protests, whether it was artillery weapons or other, whether small arms fire, how many protests. But we've already discussed the reaction, the response, and the work of teams on the mission in the case that involved me. But it was not a protest dealing with fire from small arms, from in-country weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But were such teams also formed if the complaints were about small arms fire, more specifically what is called sniping, apart from whether this was done with a weapon with an optical sight or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say whether a team was formed on every occasion because it was mostly combat operations. But I know that a team would be formed if a protest had been lodged in case of a cease-fire, so-called truce, when also we lodged the largest number of protests to the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question would be: You told us about meetings that took place where General Mladic was present, and I'm just seeking to clarify your testimony. You said that you had a clear recollection of one of these meetings, in September 1992 at Jahorina, and you also told us that the majority of such meetings were held in Lukavica. Could you tell us approximately how many Lukavica meetings where General Mladic was present have taken place in your presence. Approximately. I'm not asking whether it was -- if it was an exact number, but approximately, since you said the majority.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember meetings when General Mladic was present when I was there, and that is why I said I was quite sure about that meeting in September 1992 on Jahorina, and I'd really not be able to speak about my presence at meetings where General Mladic was, when we were in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- That the majority took place in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I did. But I did not say that General Mladic was present. I pointed out that as a rule some representatives of the main staff were present, and I remember that General Mladic attended one of those meetings on Jahorina. I'm not aware of his presence at Lukavica, but I do know that other representatives were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just read your answers to the questions in that respect. You said, "At those meetings of ours which took place on a daily basis, no, General Mladic did not appear. But I did see General Mladic at meetings when there were reports from all commanders of the brigades and regiments. General Mladic would come to some of those meetings or some of the officers from the main staff." The next question was: "Where were those meetings held in the relevant period, Pale, Lukavica, at different places, where?" You said, "In Lukavica, one was held. In Jahorina, at that time we didn't have such meetings in Pale. Mainly in Lukavica. The majority of meetings took place in Lukavica." So you're using the plural several times also in respect of meetings where General Mladic was present. Could you -- do you say your answer was not correct, or could you otherwise give me an approximate number of meetings held in Lukavica where General Mladic was present? You said General Mladic would come to some of these meetings. That's a plural.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You defined it correctly. But I was not wrong either. I said that I was present at a meeting, at a briefing on Jahorina, that meetings were held in Lukavica, and perhaps as you said, in plural, General Mladic was present. I was not present at those meetings because our commander's position was to attend to other business whilst those meetings were held, so I was not physically present there because it was more interesting and more necessary for one of the assistants to be present. And I, when I was not on the ground, I was in the operations centre, because I told you that I spent most of my time there. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I may stop you. You said, "But I did see General Mladic at meetings," also in the plural. So your testimony, as I read it from the transcript, was not that you heard about his presence but that you did see him.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw -- I did not have to be present at a meeting because the hole in our command was next to the operation centre. It was interesting for me to see who was coming. So I could see General Mladic at the meeting but I was not at the meeting. Or sometimes during the meetings if I was on duty or if it was an urgent message, then it was my duty to enter the room with a meeting and to inform the corps command about a certain message that had arrived and which needed to be acted upon immediately. So I did have the opportunity to see General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that at several occasions you saw General Mladic attending a meeting or about to attend a meeting in Lukavica; is that correct? Meetings with General Galic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then you briefly referred to the fact that although from your side it was offered to participate in the incident on the Markale market, that you were refused to participate in such a joint investigation, and you also briefly referred to your investigations. What was investigated precisely within the organisation you worked in on the Markale market incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with the market investigation. I said that I was involved in investigation of the tower, of the control tower at the airport, but it had nothing to do with Markale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't say that you participated in this investigation but referred to the refusal to allow your people to participate in a joint investigation and you briefly referred to what you called "our investigation," not saying that you participated in it. What do you know about your -- not you personally but the investigation on your side on the Markale market incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about it because as our contribution to cooperation on the ground and our relations with UNPROFOR, that day I wrote the combat report for the main staff and one item in that report contained the explanation which I had received from the liaison officer, and that report in that part -- that part of the report said that we had offered to assign a certain number of our men to the joint team of the -- the foreign investigation team, that the other side refused that, and I sent this report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I referred to that, that the other side refused your contribution to such an investigation. You said you did write the combat report of that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you explained. What did you actually explain in that report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just as I have told you: That following the protest lodged regarding the action of our forces against Markale, or rather, this destruction that was thrashed a lot by the media, that then the chief of staff set up a commission and through the liaison officer suggested that the joint commission be set up under the UNPROFOR leadership. However, the other side did not accept our proposal and that was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not want to interrupt you, but just to say that the witness said -- spoke a condition regarding the Markale incident, and this does not appear in the English transcript, and I simply wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I do understand that a commission was formed and that it was offered that this commission would take part in the investigation, a joint investigation, and it was refused. Was there any investigation either by this committee or by any other committee or any other persons investigating the alleged facts underlying the events as they were told to you? I mean, what did your part investigate -- were not allowed to participate in a joint investigation. What did your part investigate itself? Who did it and how was it done? If you have any knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say I do. All I can say is that it was discussed whether it was possible that a piece of weapon, one shell caused injuries to so many people and that, therefore, that was impossible. Now, whether a commission was formed and at which level it was discussed, I did not take part in such discussions and I, therefore, cannot speak about details. All I can say is that in general on the basis of knowledge which official -- and there was some -- official information, that it was impossible that such a thing could have happened on the basis of action of any of our pieces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "All I can say, that it was discussed whether it was possible that a piece of weapon, one shell caused injuries to so many people." Discussed by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Discussed by the whole command and all the commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that you were present during these discussions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were discussions day in, day out. Besides, the media flooded us from all sides with the footage which we simply did not believe. We simply did not believe they were authentic. We simply did not think that they were true. That is what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just told us that the conclusions drawn was that such a piece of weapon -- that one shell could not have caused so many injuries and casualties as you were told there had been. Were there any other conclusions from that -- from these discussions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other conclusions; namely, that it could have only been the result of purposeful activity of the other side orchestrated, set up, because we saw such footage. I believe this Tribunal also has some of this footage. And it is impossible not to see that along a stall three or four people are lying in pools of blood and that the stall and what is on it, the goods, the stuff that is being sold, that it is absolutely intact, that not a single scratch is there. So it's obvious that it is a set-up. These are some of the conclusions which we drew from it, and I believe such conclusions are still drawn from that because there is some such footage. I did see some of it on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What were the other sources on which you based your conclusions during these discussions? Because you told us that from the footage, you saw pictures that, as you were told, were taken from the Markale market. Were there any other sources that would support the conclusions you'd drawn at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first conclusion has to do with the action of the weapon, or rather, the shell because technically it is impossible for one shell to produce so many casualties. Had it been a bomb, I mean, dropped from the air, it could -- yes, it could cause so many casualties, because I saw such a shell, 120-millimetre shell fall next to me, and I and all the men who were working with me got off without a single scratch, whereas it fell right next to me on the asphalt and I got away completely unscathed and the men next to me, and it was only 6 metres from me. And the crater of the shell was like this, as a plate in the asphalt. And that a shell could get through all those stalls and kill so many people, it is impossible. Even a Kacusak [phoen] couldn't have done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any other considerations that were -- that you used when reaching such a conclusion in your discussions that it -- these were false allegations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you have just said, these are false accusations, and as I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have said, a set-up, and I'd rather not discuss it any further, because I really do not know. What else could I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just repeating your words that these are false allegations. I'm refraining from whether they are false or true. That's finally one of the tasks this Chamber still has to achieve. But I do understand that you cannot give me other reasons you've taken into consideration when reaching such conclusions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. I have no further questions. Are there any additional questions to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence does have a certain number of questions, yes. We'd like to finish, but we're afraid that this witness might be called tomorrow. But we shall try to be as brief as possible so as not to have to do it. Can I start?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take up the questions in a certain order and I will be precise. Could the witness be shown the map which he marked following questions by Judge Nieto-Navia, and I would like to concentrate on the airport, the area of the airport. Further examination by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were asked by Judge Nieto-Navia about the positions which was at the far east end of the airport which couldn't or could open fire in the direction of the airport. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you tell us, what were the positions facing those Serb positions that you mentioned? What were the enemy positions at the far east end of the airport?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their positions were along this line of separation, as I said, between Dobrinja I and IV on our side, Dobrinja II and III from the Muslim side, and further into depth --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will interrupt you here. I will interrupt you now, witness. The witness is adding his gesture to his words and is pointing towards Dobrinja -- or rather, the whole route which covers the complex of the airport to the north of it and, therefore, south of the Dobrinja locality. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Secondly, the enemy positions were in the area of Donji Kotorac, from the sports air field where we see this first structure - I am pointing at it here - through the locality of Donji Kotorac and then on towards the end of the runway. So these were the Muslim positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please wait for the witness to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're requested to make a break between answer and the next question. And since this courtroom has to be used this afternoon, could you please find a moment to finish in one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't do it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Conclude not your examination but for this very moment. I'm not limiting at this moment your time to ask questions to the witness but we have to continue tomorrow so --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, of course. Of course. Yes, thank you. Thank you. I shall be happy to do that. So I will repeat what I said for the transcript, and that was the witness mentioned different localities, but apart from that he extends he has gesture in the direction to the west and south of the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us what were the positions of the two sides. Do you know if there were exchanges of fire or cross-fire between these positions? And if so, often did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP35 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were exchanges of fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this -- this question and indeed the previous questions do not arise out of questions asked by you, Mr. President, and Your Honours. In any event, there has been a considerable volume of evidence to the same effect by other witnesses. So I object to this question and to the line of questioning, in terms of it -- whether it should be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you would give it some thought, what arises from questions from the Judges and what not. The mere fact that something is mentioned does not automatically mean that it's an issue that came up. But we have to adjourn anyhow, so plenty of time to consider it and then we'll hear your next questions tomorrow morning. Unfortunately we could not finish with your testimony today, Mr. DP35. But certainly we'll finish tomorrow. So I have to ask you to come back now in this same courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning.
